g.text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in scenarios
requiring continual adaptation to new tasks and domains (Wu et al., 2024;
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=2) Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in scenarios requiring continual adaptation to new tasks and domains (Wu et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024).

g.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2021)
enable efficient adaptation by training low-rank matrices while keeping base
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) enable efficient adaptation by training low-rank matrices while keeping base model weights frozen.

g.text: However, sequential fine-tuning on multiple tasks leads to catastrophic
forgetting, where performance on earlier tasks degrades as the model adapts
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=1) However, sequential fine-tuning on multiple tasks leads to catastrophic forgetting, where performance on earlier tasks degrades as the model adapts to new ones (Kirkpatrick et al., 2016).

g.text: Existing approaches to mitigate forgetting in continual learning fall into
g.title: N4 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) Existing approaches to mitigate forgetting in continual learning fall into three paradigms, each with limitations.

g.text: Regularization methods (Kirkpatrick et al., 2016; Li & Hoiem,
2016) constrain parameter updates during training but add
g.title: N4a [Prior_Work: paradigm-1] (cites=2) Regularization methods (Kirkpatrick et al., 2016; Li & Hoiem, 2016) constrain parameter updates during training but add computational overhead.

g.text: Replay-based methods (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017; Buzzega et al.,
2020) achieve strong performance by revisiting earlier examples
g.title: N4b [Prior_Work: paradigm-2] (cites=2) Replay-based methods (Lopez-Paz & Ranzato, 2017; Buzzega et al., 2020) achieve strong performance by revisiting earlier examples but require storing training data.

g.text: Architecture-based methods (Razdaibiedina et al., 2023; Wang et
al., 2023) expand model capacity per task but increase model size.
g.title: N4c [Prior_Work: paradigm-3] (cites=2) Architecture-based methods (Razdaibiedina et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023) expand model capacity per task but increase model size.

g.text: All these approaches modify the training process itself, adding complexity
g.title: N5 [Limitation] (cites=0) All these approaches modify the training process itself, adding complexity to the fine-tuning pipeline.

g.text: We propose a different perspective: rather than modifying training, we
intervene after each task to correct unintended parameter changes.
g.title: N6 [Method] (cites=0) We propose a different perspective: rather than modifying training, we intervene after each task to correct unintended parameter changes.

g.text: Insight: not all changes equally harmful
Our key insight is that not all parameter changes during fine-tuning are
g.title: N7 [Method] (cites=0) Our key insight is that not all parameter changes during fine-tuning are equally harmful.

g.text: Some attention heads undergo large changes that are not necessary for the
g.title: N8 [Method] (cites=0) Some attention heads undergo large changes that are not necessary for the new task—they are unintentionally disrupted.

g.text: These heads can be identified by three properties: high disruption (large
parameter change), high historical importance (critical for earlier tasks),
and low new-task importance (not needed for the current task).
g.title: N9 [Method] (cites=0) These heads can be identified by three properties: high disruption (large parameter change), high historical importance (critical for earlier tasks), and low new-task importance (not needed for the current task).

g.text: Rolling back these heads should recover earlier-task performance without
g.title: N10 [Method] (cites=0) Rolling back these heads should recover earlier-task performance without harming current-task accuracy.

g.text: We introduce HeadRollback, a simple post-task intervention that identifies
unintentionally disrupted attention heads and rolls back their LoRA B-matrix
g.title: N11 [Method] (cites=0) We introduce HeadRollback, a simple post-task intervention that identifies unintentionally disrupted attention heads and rolls back their LoRA B-matrix rows to the previous checkpoint.

g.text: We propose HeadRollback, a replay-free post-task
intervention for continual LoRA fine-tuning that
operates at task boundaries without modifying training
g.title: C1 [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose HeadRollback, a replay-free post-task intervention for continual LoRA fine-tuning that operates at task boundaries without modifying training dynamics.

g.text: We develop a three-signal scoring formula combining
new-task importance to identify heads worth preserving.
g.title: C2 [Contribution] (cites=0) We develop a three-signal scoring formula combining disruption magnitude, historical importance, and new-task importance to identify heads worth preserving.

g.text: We demonstrate that HeadRollback improves Overall
Performance by +1.98pp and Backward Transfer by +1.70pp
over Vanilla LoRA on a 5-task benchmark, with
consistent improvements across task orders (7/9 win…
g.title: C3 [Contribution] (cites=0) We demonstrate that HeadRollback improves Overall Performance by +1.98pp and Backward Transfer by +1.70pp over Vanilla LoRA on a 5-task benchmark, with consistent improvements across task orders (7/9 win rate).

g.text: We provide analysis showing that HeadRollback selects
heads with 3–7× higher historical importance than
disruption-only selection, and that middle layers are
g.title: C4 [Contribution] (cites=0) We provide analysis showing that HeadRollback selects heads with 3–7× higher historical importance than disruption-only selection, and that middle layers are most susceptible to unintentional disruption.
